newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Pyramid schemes promise high returns to Albanians.
newsitem.headline: Pyramid schemes promise high returns to Albanians.

text.p: Pyramid schemes, pledging big returns on small investments, have mushroomed across Albania, shaking consumer spending, distorting currency markets and ringing alarms bells at the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Bankers say the wealth the schemes offer is an illusion and warn that the system could collapse inwards, robbing ordinary people of their savings and paralysing the economy.
The World Bank has expressed its concern and last week an IMF delegation arrived in Europe's poorest country to scrutinise the business, well-placed sources said.
"There is a marvellous beginning but a disastrous end for the people participating in (pyramid schemes)," a bank official told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Pyramid schemes began springing up about three years ago as young companies sought cash that the former Stalinist state's overstretched banking system could not supply.
"The companies lacked money to invest and so they turned to the pyramid schemes. They will go on until they consider they have raised enough," the bank official said.
Today numerous firms in the impoverished Balkan country are prepared to offer interest rates of up to 50 percent a month on short-term loans.
Albanians, many of them living hand to mouth, have scrambled to hand over their hard-won savings, even selling their homes and livestock in order to join the goldrush.
The domestic press reported on Wednesday that retail sales had fallen by almost half in recent days.
"People think twice before buying normal food products," said a Tirana shop owner. "They always look for the cheapest goods so they have more left over for the pyramid schemes."
Many Albanians working abroad send their wages home so their families can buy leks to invest in the schemes, adding to a dizzying rally by the lek against western currencies this year.
On Wednesday the dollar was quoted a shade below 100 leks -- not far off the Albanian currency's recent two-year high.
Earlier this month the dollar traded down to 95 leks, compared with 117 at the start of the year.
The government has said it is looking at ways of controlling the schemes, but so far has taken little action to end the queues of hopefuls outside the company offices.
